doc_summary: The paper studies adversarially filtered and model-in-the-loop evaluation sets, finding they are harder but can yield unstable model rankings, disproportionately penalize the adversary model, and oversample low-agreement examples. It argues that difficulty alone does not make a fair or valid measure, and that adversarial sets must still reflect the core capability being measured.

items.claim: Prefers evaluation sets that still accurately reflect the target capability over sets that are merely harder, because narrow optimization against a particular model stops measuring the intended ability.
items.quote: In the extreme, adversarial datasets may be so narrowly optimized toward stumping a particular model that they no longer accurately measure the abilities that the dataset was designed to test.

items.claim: Prefers evaluating across a wide range of models over measuring difficulty with the adversary model itself, because the adversary is disproportionately affected and difficulty is overstated.
items.quote: For now, we recommend that researchers evaluate against a wide range of models where possible, and avoid measuring the difficulty of adversarial datasets using the adversary models themselves.

items.claim: Distrusts adversarially built evaluation sets as unbiased measures, since they can be unduly hard for the model class they were targeted at but not for others.
items.quote: an adversarially constructed dataset that targets a specific model may bias the resulting data, creating datasets that may be unduly challenging for one class of models but not others.

items.claim: Checks for self-targeting bias by comparing an item's rank with and without the adversary being the same model as the evaluated one; a fair set should show zero rank change.
items.quote: Ideally, if there is no model-specific bias to the filtering, there should be no change in model ranking, at the difference should be zero.

items.claim: Treats converging signals (lower model accuracy plus lower annotator agreement) as good evidence that a procedure selects hard examples, while noting that the cause of the difficulty stays ambiguous.
items.quote: Combined with our results above on lower model performance on filtered datasets, we take this as good evidence that the AFLite procedure indeed selects for the most challenging examples.

items.claim: Distrusts simple accuracy on contentious or ambiguous items, because collapsing a distribution of human labels to one label makes scores misleading.
items.quote: the current format of scoring models on simple accuracy is an inadequate method of evaluating on these low-agreement examples, as the distribution of labels is reduced to a single label based on a majority vote.

items.claim: Offers multiple competing explanations for a surprising result (rank instability) rather than committing to one, e.g. a real flaw versus an expected noise effect near chance.
items.quote: An alternative interpretation is that as stronger adversary models are used, a larger proportion of remaining examples are challenging and therefore models are more likely to perform at chance on them.

items.claim: Limits claims when evidence is thin (few adversarially collected datasets) rather than overgeneralizing, because the sample cannot support strong conclusions.
items.quote: Hence we are unable to draw strong conclusions about the efficacy of adversarial data collection for evaluation data from the current set of results.

items.claim: Chooses test tasks by explicit criteria, including that no model-adversarial procedure was already applied, to avoid confounds.
items.quote: These tasks are chosen based on several criteria: having a large enough training set to be suitable for AFLite, being in a format suitable for AFLite (i.e. classification), and no model-adversarial procedure already having been applied

items.claim: Proposes ensembling diverse adversary models or weighting examples to reduce adversary-specific bias, while acknowledging cost and that low-agreement oversampling would remain.
items.quote: a possible alternative is to ensemble a diverse set of adversary models during the AFLite algorithm, or weight examples based on the AFLite example selection based on each adversary.

items.claim: Flags that the nature of adversarial examples (what is adversarial and why it is hard) remains uninvestigated beyond performance and agreement.
items.quote: this work has not investigated the nature of the adversarial examples outside of the impact on model performance and annotator agreement.
